transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I’m Dr. [Name], and I’ll be talking with you today. What brings you in? Is there something specific you’d like to discuss?

I suppose it’s… it’s spiders, really. I feel a bit silly saying it out loud, because I’m a teacher and I can manage a classroom full of teenagers perfectly well, but at home I’ve started arranging everything around not having to see one.

Like, I put off doing laundry because the machines are in the basement, and I avoid the garden shed completely. I used to do little jobs myself—getting tools, moving boxes, that sort of thing—but now I’ll actually pay someone to do them just so I don’t have to go into those spaces. It’s become a bit ridiculous, and I don’t seem to be able to make myself just go in and get on with it.
So you mentioned spiders—when you see one, or even think about seeing one, what kind of feelings come up for you? Do you feel intense fear or panic right away?

Yes—right away, really. If I actually see one, my chest sort of clamps up immediately, and my hands start shaking. It’s ridiculous because I can stand in front of thirty Year 10s making excuses about homework and not blink, but one spider in a corner and I’m just… stuck.

Sometimes I freeze in the doorway, like I can’t make my feet move. Other times I’m backing out before I’ve even properly thought about it, as if my body’s already decided, “Nope, we’re leaving.”
